description:
Team X is a technology-driven team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge Ulaanbaatar 2026.

Our project, PARALLAX X, explores AI-powered Earth–Mars terrain analysis, planetary analog discovery, and interactive 3D rover simulation using real space agency data.

We aim to combine machine learning, scientific research, software engineering, and creative design into an innovative solution for future space exploration.
summary:
Where on Earth should we prepare for Mars? PARALLAX X transforms planetary elevation data into an immersive, evidence-driven platform for exploring terrestrial analog candidates and designing rover field experiments.

Using NASA and partner datasets, we analyzed wind-carved terrain in Mars’s Medusae Fossae Formation through five quantitative terrain features and Wasserstein-1 distance, comparing them against 1,915 Earth terrain windows. Our search identified five exploratory candidate clusters in Mongolia’s Gobi Desert.

PARALLAX X brings planetary science to life through interactive, matched-scale 3D Mars–Earth comparisons, a detailed animated rover exploring real HiRISE terrain, and transparent scientific analytics.

Beyond visualization, our Expedition Lab translates terrain evidence into proposed experiments for rover mobility, rock sampling, and thermal-energy operations, identifying what scientists must measure before field testing.

Our pre-registered validation revealed the limitations of terrain-only matching: candidate sites are not confirmed geological analogs.

By connecting real planetary data, mathematical analysis, immersive exploration, and actionable experimental planning, PARALLAX X helps turn the search for Earth analogs into a more rigorous foundation for future Mars exploration.
details:
PARALLAX X — From Planetary Terrain to Testable Rover Expeditions

Explore two worlds. Measure the difference. Plan the next experiment.

The Problem

Where on Earth should we prepare for the challenges of exploring Mars?

Terrestrial analog sites are essential for planetary research. They help scientists investigate environments resembling other planets and provide places to rehearse exploration techniques before real missions.

But visual resemblance has a critical limitation. Two landscapes may share similar ridges, slopes, and topographic patterns while differing in geological origin, surface material, soil strength, and rover mobility.

PARALLAX X addresses the gap between identifying a potentially interesting Earth location and knowing what to investigate there.

Our Solution: WHERE → WHY → WHAT NEXT

PARALLAX X is an interactive Mars–Earth terrain research platform that combines real planetary elevation data, quantitative terrain analysis, high-fidelity 3D visualization, and structured rover field-experiment planning.

It follows one connected scientific workflow:

WHERE? — Identify promising Earth research candidates.

We study wind-eroded yardang terrain in Mars's Medusae Fossae Formation using a digital terrain model derived from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX observations.

Our Python research pipeline processes this Martian terrain and NASADEM elevation data on a shared 30-metre analysis grid. We compare five topographic features: local relief, slope at 180 metres, slope at 600 metres, topographic position, and ridge coherence.

To compare entire feature distributions, we use empirical cumulative distribution normalization and Wasserstein-1 distance from optimal transport theory.

The search evaluates 1,915 pre-declared Earth terrain windows across two study domains: Mongolia's Trans-Altai Gobi and Iran's Lut Desert. It produces five exploratory Gobi candidate clusters, G-1 through G-5.

These are candidate locations for further investigation, not confirmed geological analogs.

WHY? — Understand the measurements and their limitations.

Users can compare real Mars and Earth terrain side by side in matched-scale 3D, inspect feature distances and terrain profiles, and explore the mathematical evidence underlying candidate rankings.

Our separate high-resolution NASA HiRISE scene demonstrates why measurement scale matters: within the same studied Martian terrain crop, the area exceeding a 15-degree slope changes from 13.9% at an approximately 4-metre measurement baseline to 1.6% at 180 metres.

The landscape does not change; the resolution of the question changes.

Our original screening method was pre-registered and tested against known terrestrial yardang fields, negative controls, and a simpler slope-only baseline. It did not meet the pre-defined validation criteria. We preserve this outcome rather than treating high-ranked candidates as proven analogs.

This distinction is fundamental to PARALLAX X: terrain similarity can suggest useful research questions, but it cannot independently establish geological equivalence or rover safety.

WHAT NEXT? — Design a real rover field experiment.

Our signature feature, Expedition Lab, transforms a selected candidate and its available terrain evidence into a structured field-investigation plan.

It supports three experimental objectives:

  1. Wheel Mobility: Plan measurements of wheel slip, traction, sinkage, route inclination, soil properties, and energy consumption.
  2. Rock Sampling and Drilling: Define the geological observations, instruments, and material tests needed to investigate sampling operations.
  3. Thermal and Energy Operations: Plan the environmental and electrical measurements required to study rover operating conditions.

Each protocol specifies a research objective, hypothesis, available evidence, required equipment, measurements, repeatable procedures, quality checks, and scientific limitations.

Missing physical properties are explicitly marked NOT MEASURED. The protocols are proposals for future fieldwork; no physical field trials are claimed.

An Immersive Rover Experience

PARALLAX X also features an interactive six-wheel expedition rover on a separate, high-resolution HiRISE-derived Martian terrain scene.

The 3D experience includes terrain-following movement, independently animated wheels, a moving camera mast, cinematic perspectives, and a linked terrain profile.

We adapted NASA/JPL-Caltech's publicly available Perseverance 3D model, removed protected insignia, optimized its geometry and textures for browser performance, and implemented the interactive animation.

The rover illustrates terrain-scale questions and exploration workflows. It is not a validated physical mobility simulation, and its illustrative path does not establish that any Earth candidate is safe to traverse.

Technical Implementation

PARALLAX X combines:

  • Scientific computing: Python, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, geospatial reprojection, deterministic terrain-feature extraction, empirical distributions, and Wasserstein distance.
  • Web platform: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Three.js, WebGL, Tailwind CSS, and interactive terrain visualization.
  • Planetary datasets: NASA PDS HiRISE, NASADEM, Mars CTX-derived terrain, MOLA, Copernicus DEM GLO-30, and ESA WorldCover.
  • Reproducibility: Pre-registered scientific rules, documented data provenance, numerical tests, a slope-only comparison baseline, and publicly available source code.

Raster processing and terrain analysis are performed offline. The public application is statically deployed, with no dedicated backend and no runtime AI API required for candidate ranking or experiment planning.

The project is a software research prototype; it does not include newly manufactured rover hardware.

Creativity and Impact

Our creative contribution is not simply displaying Mars in 3D or assigning Earth locations a similarity score.

It is connecting discovery, evidence, uncertainty, and experimental design in one interactive research experience.

Instead of presenting visually similar landscapes as final answers, PARALLAX X helps users understand what satellite data can reveal and what must still be measured.

For planetary researchers, it offers a reproducible starting point for investigating terrestrial terrain candidates.

For rover engineers and field teams, it converts remote-sensing observations into concrete questions about mobility, sampling, and operating conditions.

For students and educators, it makes planetary remote sensing, applied mathematics, and robotics more accessible through genuine data-driven visualization.

A future development path is to incorporate higher-resolution terrestrial surveys and real field measurements, allowing researchers to evaluate candidate sites beyond regional topography.

Our vision is to turn the question "Where on Earth looks like Mars?" into a more useful one: "What can we investigate there, why does it matter, and what evidence do we need next?"
